demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
avoid anything that could be stressful
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: The denial/minimisation in Magical Thinking sits awkwardly with the very global, entrenched negative self-change appraisals. A patient who mainly copes by telling himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad would not typically also report such strongly elaborated identity-collapse appraisals unless there were clearer supporting items linking the trauma to guilt/shame; here the combination feels internally strained.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the negative appraisals are missing the expected guilt/responsibility/being dangerous-to-others theme. Instead they focus on global misery and identity change, which is not impossible but is a weak fit to the trauma-specific cognitive content.

vignette:
Marco sat in the intake chair with the controlled stillness of someone who had learned to hold himself together by force of will. He was twenty-two, an HVAC technician for a commercial maintenance company in Phoenix, and he had not felt like himself in nearly a year. The person he had become, he said, was unrecognisable to him. He spoke about that person as though describing a stranger he had been forced to live with.

The event that had undone him happened on a late August afternoon. Marco was servicing a rooftop unit at a strip mall. The compressor had been cycling erratically, and he had traced the problem to a faulty pressure switch. He remembered the heat coming off the black roofing membrane, the smell of hot tar and dust, the way the metal casing of the unit burned his forearm when he leaned against it. He had finished the repair, closed the access panel, and was packing his tools when he heard a shout from below. A woman who worked in the dry cleaner’s had stepped onto the back loading dock to take a smoke break. The panel he had just closed—he had not latched it properly. It had fallen. The edge of the heavy metal door struck her on the temple. She went down immediately. Marco scrambled down the ladder, calling 911, pressing a rag to her head, telling her to stay with him. She survived, but the injury left her with a traumatic brain injury and permanent cognitive deficits. Marco had not been able to return to that strip mall. He had not been able to return to any rooftop job since.

The memory of that moment was not fully his. He told his therapist that when he tried to picture it, the scene felt like something he had watched in a movie, or like a story someone else had told him about a terrible day they had lived through. It did not feel like something that had happened to his own body. And yet his body remembered it anyway. At unpredictable moments—while driving, while lying in bed, while standing in the quiet of a supply closet—the smell of hot tar and dust would flood his nose, vivid and unbidden, and the memory would force its way into his mind without warning. He could not control when it came. He could only endure it.

What frightened Marco most was what the event had revealed about himself. He had come to believe that his own body was unreliable, that he could no longer trust his hands or his judgment. He had gone over the details of that afternoon hundreds of times, replaying the sequence, searching for the exact moment he had made the mistake, trying to understand why he had not checked the latch a second time, why he had not noticed the gap, why he had not done more to stop what happened. He was certain he would never forgive himself for that failure. The person he had been before—the one who climbed onto roofs without a second thought, who trusted his training, who believed he was careful—that person was gone. In his place was someone who saw danger everywhere.

Marco had begun to avoid anything that could be stressful. He stopped taking new jobs unless he knew the building was single-story and the equipment was on the ground. He turned down work that involved ladders, or unfamiliar sites, or any situation where he could not control every variable. His supervisor had started to notice. His pay had dropped. His coworkers made jokes about him being picky, and he let them, because explaining would have meant saying it aloud. He also avoided dates and anniversaries connected to the event. The Thursday of that week, the last week of August, the exact date—he made sure he was not working on those days. He stayed home, kept the television on, tried not to think.

The only place Marco felt safe was his apartment. He had rearranged his life so that he spent as little time as possible in spaces he could not control. Even silence had become threatening. If he was in a room and the noise stopped suddenly—the hum of a refrigerator cutting out, the pause between songs on the radio—his chest would tighten and his breathing would quicken. He had come to interpret quiet as a warning. Something was about to happen. Something bad. He was always waiting for it.

What finally brought Marco to seek help was the physical reactivity he could no longer hide. At a routine service call at a hardware store, a customer dropped a metal wrench on the concrete floor. The sound was sharp and sudden. Marco dropped to his knees, heart hammering, hands shaking, covered in sweat. The store manager asked if he was okay. Marco said he was fine. He was not fine. He made it back to his truck and sat there for twenty minutes before he could drive. That night, he searched online for a therapist. He did not know if talking would help. He was afraid it would not. But he was more afraid of spending the rest of his life as this stranger, trapped in an apartment, waiting for the next thing to fall.
